content_voiceover: These photos continue the same case and add two teaching points. First, several of these bruises are large, confluent hematomas over the knee, thigh, and hip, larger than the small petechial pattern you'd expect from platelet dysfunction alone, a reminder that with more severe thrombocytopenia, platelet-type bleeding can still look impressively large even though the mechanism is still a platelet plug problem, not a coagulation factor deficiency; deep muscle or joint hemarthrosis-type bleeding still shouldn't be present. Second, one photo shows a young child with bruising on both legs, underscoring that inherited thrombocytopenias present across the lifespan, including in children, and a pediatric or lifelong bruising history should always raise suspicion for an inherited platelet disorder rather than a purely acquired process like classic adult ITP. Taken together with the prior photos, this bruising pattern, its severity, and the pediatric case are exactly the clinical picture that turns out, on the next slide, to be an MYH9-related inherited thrombocytopenia masquerading as ITP.
keypoints: Severe thrombocytopenia → large confluent bruises, not just petechiae
Pediatric/lifelong bruising history → suspect inherited platelet disorder
Sets up next case: MYH9-related disorder mimicking ITP
keypoint_voiceover: Large confluent bruises over the knee and hip show that severe thrombocytopenia can still produce big ecchymoses, not just petechiae. And bruising in a child points toward a lifelong, inherited process rather than acquired disease. This is the clinical picture behind the upcoming case of an MYH9-related inherited thrombocytopenia mimicking ITP.
